questions.title: What Does the PM Say?
questions.storyContext: The brief is done. Before Parliament sees it, the PM wants your advice. He's addressing the nation at 8am tomorrow. Six million people remember the night the lights went out — hospitals on backup generators, MRT stations going dark. They want to know if it will happen again. The PM asks: "What should I tell them?"
questions.facilitatorPrompt: Whatever he says, six million people hear it. And the full truth will eventually come out. If we say stay calm and it leaks that 12 substations were under enemy control for hours — how does that look? But if we scare people with the full picture, what does that do to confidence?

options.label: Tell them the threat was dealt with quickly and systems performed as designed. Keep it reassuring. Going into detail about 12 compromised substations risks panic over something already resolved.

Tell the truth. Singapore was attacked. 12 substations compromised. It was serious, it lasted hours. Then explain exactly how the team contained it and brought the grid back. People can handle honesty.
Acknowledge a significant cyber incident without dramatising it. Detected early, contained, full review underway. Honest about the severity without giving details that help the next attacker.
Skip attack details. Announce the $500M cybersecurity investment. Talk about what comes next. People care less about what happened and more about whether it'll happen again. Give them a plan.

questions.title: What Do We Build?
questions.storyContext: Parliament approved $500M in emergency cybersecurity funding. Your team presents the strategic direction. This isn't just a technical decision — it's about what kind of digital nation Singapore becomes. You watched the anomalous readings climb, fought the attacker inside the grid, raced to restore 200,000 homes, and built the case for Parliament. Now you decide what Singapore builds so nobody has to do what your team just did.
questions.facilitatorPrompt: Five hundred million dollars and ten years of national strategy. What was the real lesson of the blackout? Was our infrastructure too fragile? Were we too slow? Were we fighting alone when we shouldn't have been?

options.label: Lock everything down. Nothing trusted by default, even from inside government buildings. Disconnect the most sensitive systems from the internet forever. The attacker got in because there were gaps. Close every single one.

Build systems that expect to be attacked. Spread critical functions across many independent parts, add self-repairing networks, let AI handle the first wave. The blackout lasted hours because recovery was manual. Make the next one last minutes.

Singapore can't defend alone. Create a Southeast Asian cyber defence alliance — shared intelligence, joint response teams, collective defence agreements. Turn Singapore from a single target into the anchor of a regional shield.

Invest in the people. Every citizen learns basic cyber hygiene. Every business gets a security audit. Stand up a national cyber reserve corps. The best firewall is six million people who know what a phishing email looks like.
